pages.text: At a Saturday programme, a highlife band is setting up. The guitarist picks a string before the instrument is plugged in. You can hardly hear it. An electric guitar has a solid body with no hollow box to make its sound louder. Then a cable is pushed into the amplifier, the same string is picked, and a clear note rings across the whole park. The string is not louder. Something has turned its tiny movement into electricity, and the electricity has been turned back into sound. That something is a magnet wrapped in wire, and it never touches the string.

pages.text: The story begins in London in 1831. Michael Faraday pushed a magnet into a coil of wire and saw the needle of his meter flick. An electric current had flowed, although there was no battery. When he held the magnet still, nothing happened. When he pulled it out, the needle flicked the other way. Faraday had found a rule of nature: whenever the magnetic field through a coil changes, a voltage is produced in the coil. If the coil is part of a complete circuit, a current flows. This effect is called electromagnetic induction.

An electric current had flowed, although there was no battery.
When he held the magnet still, nothing happened.
When he pulled it out, the needle flicked the other way.
Faraday had found a rule of nature: whenever the magnetic field through a coil changes, a voltage is produced in the coil.
If the coil is part of a complete circuit, a current flows.
This effect is called electromagnetic induction.
pages.alt: A bar magnet being pushed into a coil of wire that is joined to a meter with a swinging needle.

pages.text: Look under the strings of an electric guitar and you will see a small bar called a pickup. Inside it are magnets with thousands of turns of fine copper wire wound round them. The strings are made of steel, a magnetic metal, so the part of each string above the pickup becomes a weak magnet itself. When the string vibrates, this little magnet moves to and fro above the coil. The magnetic field through the coil keeps changing, so a small current flows in the wire. The current rises and falls in exactly the same pattern as the string moves.

pages.alt: A close view of steel guitar strings passing over a pickup bar with a row of round metal poles.

pages.text: That current is far too small to drive a speaker. It first goes to an amplifier, which uses transistors and mains electricity to make a much larger copy. The big current then flows through a coil fixed to the paper cone of a loudspeaker. The coil sits beside a magnet, and the changing current makes it push and pull against the magnet. The cone moves with it, shakes the air, and you hear the note. Follow the energy: movement of the string, to electrical energy, to movement of the cone, to sound. Nylon strings would not work, because nylon is not magnetic.

pages.text: Now make everything bigger. At Akosombo, water from Lake Volta rushes down wide pipes and spins a turbine, a wheel with curved blades. The turbine turns a shaft, and on the shaft are powerful magnets surrounded by huge coils of copper wire. As the magnets spin, the magnetic field through the coils keeps changing, and a large current flows. This machine is a generator. Akosombo has six of them. A guitar pickup and a power station follow the same rule that Faraday found. One is driven by a fingertip and the other by a river.

One is driven by a fingertip and the other by a river.
pages.alt: A cut-away view of a dam with water flowing down a pipe to spin a turbine joined to a large generator.

pages.text: Once you know the rule, you will find it everywhere. A bicycle dynamo presses a small wheel against the tyre, and as you ride it spins a magnet inside a coil to light the lamp. A microphone has a coil that moves near a magnet when your voice shakes it. A petrol generator outside a shop spins its magnets with an engine. Wind turbines use the wind, and the stations at Aboadze use steam and hot gas. Almost all the electricity people use is made by moving magnets and coils past each other. Without Faraday’s discovery, the world would be very dark.

activities.question: What did Faraday discover in 1831?
options: A battery is needed to make any current
A changing magnetic field through a coil produces a voltage
Magnets lose their strength in coils

activities.question: Why must the strings of an electric guitar be made of steel?
options: Steel is a magnetic metal, so the string becomes a small magnet

activities.question: What does the turbine do in a hydroelectric power station?
options: It is spun by water and turns the magnets of the generator

activities.question: Apply it: A learner holds a strong magnet perfectly still inside a coil joined to a meter. What will the meter show, and why?
options: A large steady current, because the magnet is strong
No current, because the magnetic field through the coil is not changing
A current that grows slowly with time

activities.prompt: Follow one note from finger to ear. Put the steps in order.
items: A finger picks the steel string and it vibrates
The moving string changes the magnetic field through the pickup coil
A small current flows in the coil
The amplifier makes a larger copy of the current
The loudspeaker cone moves and sends out sound

activities.definition: Electromagnetic induction: the production of a voltage in a coil when the magnetic field through it changes.
distractors: The pulling of iron towards a magnet
The heating of a wire by a current

glossary.definition: A device that makes a larger copy of a small electrical signal.
Magnetic field: the region around a magnet where its force can be felt.
Electromagnetic induction: the production of a voltage in a coil when the magnetic field through it changes.
The part of an electric guitar, made of magnets and coils, that turns string movement into electric current.
A wheel with blades that is spun by moving water, steam, gas, or wind.
A machine that produces electricity by turning magnets and coils past each other.
